raw_response:
I’m 65 this year, been farming these fields since I was 20. Never spent a day in school, but I know every inch of my 16 mu of land. It’s just me and my old woman now — two mouths to feed, two pairs of hands, and neither of us young anymore. We can’t carry heavy loads like we used to, so we have to be smart and careful with what we’ve got.

**The wheat** — I plant it in the first week of October, same as always. I save my own seed from last year, so I don’t pay a fen for that. Before sowing, I disk the field after the maize comes off, then I broadcast two big scoops of compound fertilizer per mu — that’s about 20 kg. I sow with the hand-pushed seeder. Come March, when the wheat turns green, I walk the fields. If it looks a little pale — and it usually does — I spread another two scoops of urea per mu, about 20 kg. I only do it once. No time for all that fancy splitting. I irrigate twice: once before winter so the seedlings settle in, and once at jointing in April when the weather turns hot. Pumping costs money, and electricity isn’t cheap, so two times is all I can afford. I spray herbicide once in spring. In June, I hire Old Wang’s combine — my back can’t take swinging a sickle anymore. I expect about 350 kg per mu. Last year I got 360, so that’s what I’m hoping.

**The maize** — that goes in the same week the wheat comes out, mid-June. That window is tight; we work from dawn to dark. I buy hybrid seed every year — 45 yuan per mu — because you can’t save hybrid seed. I dibble the seeds into the stubble, and in each hole I put fertilizer: two and a half scoops of compound per mu, about 25 kg, and one and a half scoops of urea, about 15 kg. All at planting — no time to come back. If the summer rains are good, the maize might do fine without water, but usually I give it one good flood when the ears are forming in late July. I spray herbicide after planting. Harvest is late September. Sometimes my nephew comes to help, sometimes I hire a small machine. I’m hoping for about 380 kg per mu, maybe 400 if the year smiles on us.

Money is tight. My pension is only a little over 100 yuan a month. I spend about 6,400 yuan on inputs for the whole year, and that’s already stretching it. The extension fellow says I should use more fertilizer, but he’s not the one paying for it. I’d rather be a little short on inputs than short on cash when my old woman needs medicine. I’ve farmed this way for 45 years, and it’s kept us fed.
